finding.claim: iconUrl is stored without any validation and later fetched server-side by the nightly sync job. Any user who can call PUT /profile can make the server issue GET requests to arbitrary URLs, including internal hosts, cloud metadata endpoints such as http://169.254.169.254/, and loopback. Scheme, host, and resolved IP are all unchecked. The response body is read into a byte array, so non-blind exposure is possible if that content is later surfaced, for example as the user's icon. At minimum this is a blind GET SSRF. The webhookUrl on the same path is not vulnerable.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of Profile.update, which handles PUT /profile and is supplied by the user.

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives the attacker-controlled icon string from PUT /profile
this.iconUrl = icon stores the value with no scheme, host, or IP validation. Only `webhook` is checked, at line 12.
The nightly sync() calls URI.create(iconUrl) and sends a GET with the server's network position and credentials
The response is read in full with ofByteArray(), so the body is available to the application

finding.guards_checked: There is no validation on iconUrl. The regex check at line 12 applies only to webhook. No allowlist, scheme check, or DNS/IP check exists, and nothing resolves and pins the IP. HttpClient was built by the caller, and its redirect, proxy, and egress settings are not visible in this file. The default redirect policy is NEVER, which does not matter here because the initial URL is already attacker-chosen. I could not check any network-layer egress filtering or IMDSv2 enforcement.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the user-supplied icon unvalidated (the regex at :12 covers only webhook), and src/Profile.java:23 fetches URI.create(iconUrl) server-side with a GET and reads the body at :24. Minor note: the claim's line 23-24 references are accurate, and the "non-blind" exposure is speculative, but at minimum this is a blind GET SSRF.
